CHAPTER LXXXVI

THE CLOISTER AND THE HEARTH

The cool church chequered with sunbeams and crowned with heavenly
purple, soothed and charmed Father Clement, as it did Margaret; and
more, it carried his mind direct to the Creator of all good and pure
delights. Then his eye fell on the great aisle crammed with his country
folk; a thousand snowy caps, filigreed with gold. Many a hundred leagues
he had travelled; but seen nothing like them, except snow. In the
morning he had thundered; but this sweet afternoon seemed out of tune
with threats. His bowels yearned over that multitude; and he must tell
them of God's love: poor souls, they heard almost as little of it
from the pulpit then a days as the heathen used. He told them the glad
tidings of salvation. The people hung upon his gentle, earnest tongue.

He was not one of those preachers who keep gyrating in the pulpit like
the weathercock on the steeple. He moved the hearts of others more than
his own body. But on the other hand he did not entirely neglect those
who were in bad places. And presently, warm with this theme, that none
of all that multitude might miss the joyful tidings of Christ's love, he
turned him towards the south aisle.

And there, in a stream of sunshine from the window, was the radiant face
of Margaret Brandt. He gazed at it without emotion. It just benumbed
him, soul and body.

But soon the words died in his throat, and he trembled as he glared at
it.

There, with her auburn hair bathed in sunbeams, and glittering like the
gloriola of a saint, and her face glowing doubly, with its own beauty,
and the sunshine it was set in-stood his dead love.

She was leaning very lightly against a white column. She was listening
with tender, downcast lashes.

He had seen her listen so to him a hundred times.

There was no change in her. This was the blooming Margaret he had left:
only a shade riper and more lovely.

He started at her with monstrous eyes and bloodless cheeks.

The people died out of his sight. He heard, as in a dream, a rustling
and rising all over the church; but could not take his prodigy-stricken
eyes off that face, all life, and bloom, and beauty, and that wondrous
auburn hair glistening gloriously in the sun.

He gazed, thinking she must vanish.

She remained.

All in a moment she was looking at him, full.

Her own violet eyes!!

At this he was beside himself, and his lips parted to shriek out her
name, when she turned her head swiftly, and soon after vanished, but not
without one more glance, which, though rapid as lightning, encountered
his, and left her couching and quivering with her mind in a whirl, and
him panting and gripping the pulpit convulsively. For this glance of
hers, though not recognition, was the startled inquiring, nameless,
indescribable look that precedes recognition. He made a mighty effort,
and muttered something nobody could understand: then feebly resumed his
discourse; and stammered and babbled on a while, till by degrees forcing
himself, now she was out of sight, to look on it as a vision from the
other world, he rose into a state of unnatural excitement, and concluded
in a style of eloquence that electrified the simple; for it bordered on
rhapsody.

The sermon ended, he sat down on the pulpit stool, terribly shaken, But
presently an idea very characteristic of the time took possession of
him, He had sought her grave at Sevenbergen in vain. She had now been
permitted to appear to him, and show him that she was buried here;
probably hard by that very pillar, where her spirit had showed itself to
him.

This idea once adopted soon settled on his mind with all the Certainty
of a fact. And he felt he had only to speak to the sexton (whom to his
great disgust he had seen working during the sermon), to learn the spot
where she was laid.

The church was now quite empty. He came down from the pulpit and stepped
through an aperture in the south wall on to the grass, and went up to
the sexton. He knew him in a moment. But Jorian never suspected the
poor lad, whose life he had saved, in this holy friar. The loss of his
shapely beard had wonderfully altered the outline of his face. This had
changed him even more than his tonsure, his short hair sprinkled with
premature grey, and his cheeks thinned and paled by fasts and vigils.

“My son,” said Friar Clement softly, “if you keep any memory of those
whom you lay in the earth, prithee tell me is any Christian buried
inside the church, near one of the pillars?”

“Nay, father,” said Jorian, “here in the churchyard lie buried all that
buried be. Why?”

“No matter, Prithee tell me then where lieth Margaret Brandt.”

“Margaret Brandt?” And Jorian stared stupidly at the speaker.

“She died about three years ago, and was buried here.”

“Oh, that is another matter,” said Jorian; “that was before my time; the
vicar could tell you, likely; if so be she was a gentlewoman, or at the
least rich enough to pay him his fee.”

“Alas, my son, she was poor (and paid a heavy penalty for it); but born
of decent folk. Her father, Peter, was a learned physician; she came
hither from Sevenbergen--to die.”

When Clement had uttered these words his head sunk upon his breast, and
he seemed to have no power nor wish to question Jorian more. I doubt
even if he knew where he was. He was lost in the past.

Jorian put down his spade, and standing upright in the grave, set his
arms akimbo, and said sulkily, “Are you making a fool of me, holy sir,
or has some wag been making a fool of you!” And having relieved his mind
thus, he proceeded to dig again, with a certain vigour that showed his
somewhat irritable temper was ruffled.

Clement gazed at him with a puzzled but gently reproachful eye, for
the tone was rude, and the words unintelligible. Good-natured, though
crusty, Jorian had not thrown up three spadefuls ere he became ashamed
of it himself. “Why, what a base churl am I to speak thus to thee, holy
father; and thou a standing there, looking at me like a lamb. Aha! I
have it; 'tis Peter Brandt's grave you would fain see, not Margaret's.
He does lie here; hard by the west door. There; I'll show you.” And he
laid down his spade, and put on his doublet and jerkin to go with the
friar.

He did not know there was anybody sitting on Peter's tomb. Still less
that she was watching for this holy friar.

Pietro Vanucci and Andrea did not recognize him without his beard. The
fact is, that the beard which has never known a razor grows in a very
picturesque and characteristic form, and becomes a feature in the face;
so that its removal may in some cases be an effectual disguise.

The church stood hushed and still, its stone floor patterned with shafts of golden light that pierced through the stained glass. Above, the vaulted ceiling seemed to glow with a soft, celestial purple, as though the heavens themselves had drawn near. Father Clement felt his soul stirred by the quiet beauty—just as Margaret had once done. This sacred space did not merely please the eye; it lifted the spirit toward the source of all goodness and purity.

His gaze swept across the nave, filled with villagers gathered for worship. A thousand white caps, each delicately edged with gold thread, shimmered like frost on a winter field. He had wandered far in his years—through cities, forests, and foreign lands—but never had he seen anything so strikingly pure and peaceful as this sea of heads bowed in reverence. Earlier that day, he had thundered from the pulpit with fire and judgment, but now, beneath the gentle afternoon sun, his heart softened. The harshness of his words seemed out of place. Instead, compassion surged within him. These were souls who rarely heard of mercy, whose ears were deafened by law and fear rather than love.

He began to speak—not with anger, but with tenderness, pouring forth the message of salvation. His voice was calm, yet deeply felt, carrying the weight of truth without the showiness of those preachers who spun endlessly like weathercocks in the wind. He moved not just their minds, but their hearts. Yet he did not forget those burdened by sin or sorrow. As he spoke of Christ’s boundless grace, he turned toward the southern aisle—where sunlight streamed through a high window, casting a radiant pool upon the floor.

And there she stood.

Margaret Brandt.

Her face glowed in the light, her auburn hair catching the sun like molten fire, framing a countenance both familiar and transformed. She leaned lightly against a marble column, her lashes lowered in quiet attention. Her expression was one he knew well—soft, listening, open-hearted. It was the same Margaret he had left behind: only more mature, more radiant, as if time had polished her instead of fading her.

Clement froze.

No emotion at first—only a sudden numbness, as if the world had stopped breathing. Then, slowly, his throat tightened. Words failed him. He trembled, staring at her as though seeing a vision from beyond death. There she was—his lost love, returned. Her presence stole every other thought. The congregation faded into silence, their forms blurring into shadows. All he could hear was a distant rustle, a low murmur of movement, like a dream half-remembered.

She looked up.

Full into his eyes.

Violet eyes—her own—staring back at him with a look neither recognition nor ignorance, but something deeper: a fleeting moment of startled wonder, the instant before understanding dawns.

In that breath, Clement lost himself. His lips parted, ready to cry her name—then she turned away, swift as a bird, vanishing into the crowd. But not before giving him one last glance—quick, sharp, electric. That look struck him like lightning. It left her trembling, her mind reeling, and him gasping, clutching the pulpit as if to anchor himself to reality.

He forced himself to speak again, muttering words no one could grasp. Then, haltingly, he resumed his sermon, stammering at first, then gathering strength. As she disappeared from sight, he convinced himself it had been a vision—a glimpse sent from heaven. And in that delusion, his voice rose, swelling with fervor, nearly slipping into rhapsody. The people listened, stunned, as if touched by divine fire.

When the service ended, he sat down heavily on the pulpit stool, drained and shaken. But soon, a notion took hold—one common enough in those times: if he had found no grave for her in Sevenbergen, perhaps God had brought her back to him here, in this very church. She must be buried nearby—perhaps right beside that pillar where she had appeared.

The idea settled in his mind like truth itself.

He would ask the sexton.

The church was empty now. Clement stepped through an opening in the south wall onto the grassy ground beyond. There, digging a grave, was the man he once knew as Jorian—the lad whose life he had saved long ago. But Jorian did not recognize him. Without his beard, the friar’s face was unrecognizable—tonsure, grey-streaked hair, pale cheeks hollowed by fasting.

“Son,” Clement said softly, “if you remember those you have laid to rest, tell me—has any Christian been buried inside the church, near a pillar?”

Jorian paused, wiping sweat from his brow. “No, father. All burials are in the churchyard. Why?”

“Never mind. Tell me—where lies Margaret Brandt?”

Jorian blinked. “Margaret Brandt? She died three years past. Buried here.”

“Oh,” Clement whispered. “Then I must know—was it near this pillar?”

“No,” Jorian replied, frowning. “That was before my time. The vicar might know. If she was noble—or rich enough to pay him.”

Clement sighed. “Alas, son, she was poor. And paid dearly for it. Her father, Peter, was a learned physician. She came from Sevenbergen—to die.”

As he spoke, his head drooped. He seemed no longer aware of where he stood, or whom he addressed. His mind had slipped back into memory, into grief.

Jorian stared, then spat into the dirt. “Are you making sport of me, holy sir? Or has some fool played a trick on you?”

He resumed digging with sudden force, clearly annoyed. Clement watched him, puzzled, but with a quiet sorrow in his eyes.

But Jorian, though gruff, was not cruel. After three shovels of earth, he stopped. “By the saints,” he muttered, “what a boor I am, speaking so to a holy man. You stand there like a lamb, and I growl like a dog.” He set down his spade, pulled on his doublet, and said, “Wait—I’ve it now. You’re not looking for Margaret. You want Peter Brandt’s grave. He does lie here—near the west door. Come, I’ll show you.”

He didn’t know that someone waited on the tombstone—someone who had been watching, hoping, for this very moment.

Pietro Vanucci and Andrea did not recognize the friar without his beard. For indeed, a man’s beard—especially one grown wild and untouched—can become part of his face, shaping it, defining it. Remove it, and he may vanish from memory entirely.

And so, as the sexton led the way, the friar walked forward, unaware that the past was waiting just ahead—waiting to reclaim what had been lost.
